Once the thought starts, I get really shaky, my heart races, I feel almost lightheaded, like I’m about to pass out. At home I keep checking the stove knobs and the front door lock repeatedly before bed, because I’m terrified I’ll somehow leave something on, make a gas leak, or be too sick to wake up if there’s a fire. For the past couple of years, I’ve been constantly worried that there’s something seriously wrong with my body. It jumps around—one month I’m convinced I have cancer, then it’s a brain tumor, then some rare autoimmune thing I read about while researching a client’s book. It’s not just one disease; it’s like anything I come across online or in a manuscript can become the new “thing” I’m sure I have.

Once the idea gets in my head, it doesn’t let go. I end up checking my body over and over—feeling for lumps, staring at moles, taking my temperature several times a day. I keep rereading the same medical articles, comparing symptoms line by line. If I try to stop, the fear spikes. My heart races, I get sweaty, my chest feels tight, and I can’t focus on writing.

I’ve been to urgent care and my primary doctor more times than I want to admit, getting tests I don’t really need, but even normal results only calm me down for a day or so. Then a new fear starts, and I’m back to checking and researching again.
